A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VideoSafety-R1 research, and their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison. The renamed evaluation and training datasets can be matched across versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, training experiments, ablations, visual attacks, and human validation of its response evaluator in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds defense comparisons, dataset audits, cross-language evaluations, and diagnostic analyses.

M1.justification: The alarm tokens, multitask AT-SFT objective, cold-start stage, Safety-guided GRPO, and dynamic reward adaptation remain unchanged in Equations 1–6 and the training recipes. VideoSafetyThinking renames the existing VSB-R1-46k dataset. Applying the framework to Qwen2.5 VL and disclosing additional settings do not establish an algorithmic redesign.

E1.justification: v2 adds hallucination evaluation on VideoHallucer, anomaly detection on XD-Violence, and controlled evaluation with translated prompts across ten languages (Table 3 and Appendices N–O). These expand task and input-language coverage beyond v1's evaluations. The original multilingual video pool, 11.4k evaluation set, and 46k training set remain identifiable under revised names.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated defense comparators Self-Reminder, SPA-VL, VLGuard, and MM-RLHF, plus Holmes-VAD (Tables 2 and 21). The benchmark comparison expands from 14 to 21 video models, adding commercial models, InternVL3 variants, and larger Qwen2.5 VL variants. Conversely, VideoLLaMA2-7B and VideoChat2-7B disappear from the visual-attack comparison present in v1 Table 10.

E3.justification: The VLGuard-Video experiment changes from rotating images into videos to repeating static images and varying sampled frame counts from 1 to 60. v2 also introduces matched nine-frame video/thumbnail/middle-frame controls, training on Qwen2.5 VL-3B/7B, and new human-audit protocols involving 1,000 videos and 10,000 queries. Helpfulness itself already existed in v1; its human-score MSE validation is newly added.

E4.justification: Beyond retained FPS, visual-attack, and component ablations, v2 adds controlled semantic-richness tests, attention-sink analysis, video-length analysis, loss-weight sensitivity, Qwen2.5 VL ablations, reasoning-diversity measurements, and dataset-quality checks. Its case appendix replaces four examples with nineteen covering all subcategories, including a failure example and safe-query behavior. These substantially broaden the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's reported 0.81% standard deviation summarizes variation across frame-count conditions in a sensitivity experiment, rather than uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for new defenses, backbones, audits, and diagnostic experiments. The original 18.4% baseline and 89.5% defended DSR remain, while their incorrectly reported 65.1-point difference becomes 71.1 points. The headline average safety drop changes from 42.3% across 14 models to 34.2% across 21, reflecting different comparator coverage. A retained Qwen2.5 VL-7B SH result changes from 65.7% to 66.7%; rotating-video results and detailed base-LLM category rows are removed.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 retain the same objectives, reward construction, GRPO update, and evaluation definitions. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced; the added mechanism arguments are empirical interpretations.

C1.justification: v2 withdraws the prominent first-benchmark/first-investigation claims and foregrounds the existing 11.4k evaluation benchmark and 46k thinking dataset instead of the full 77,646-pair pool. It emphasizes helpful responses and qualifies preservation of general capabilities as avoiding significant compromise. The central claims about video-induced safety degradation and the dual-stage defense remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds an attention-redistribution explanation for alarm tokens, distinguishes token load from harmful semantics more explicitly, and interprets cross-language safety gains as potentially conservative behavior with reduced helpfulness. It also distinguishes safety alignment from anomaly detection and adds limitations concerning long videos and evaluator reliability under complex attacks. Some interpretations overreach: Appendix N's universal non-English improvement claim has exceptions in Tables 19–20.

D1.justification: v2 discloses previously unspecified classification and reward weights, compute/latency measurements, baseline adaptation recipes, and additional sampling information. Appendix R.6 supplies the false-negative-check prompt missing from v1's duplicated prompt listing. A repository pointer replaces the supplementary-code statement, and release restrictions are documented. Dataset availability remains internally inconsistent: the abstract says available, while the reproducibility statement says release awaits verification.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive positioning against concurrent Video-SafetyBench, SafeVid, and Trust-VideoLLMs work, replacing v1's broad priority framing. A new video-anomaly-detection discussion distinguishes that objective from response safety. Additional attention-sink and SFT-versus-RL references support the expanded mechanism discussion; these exceed bibliographic or citation-style updates.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, experimental narrative, and limitations. Dataset construction is condensed in the main text and moved into appendices, the training dataset becomes part of the method section, and helpfulness and robustness receive integrated main-text treatment. Terminology and appendix organization are extensively revised.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the main result tables to integrate safety, helpfulness, and false refusal; redisplays base-LLM comparisons as Figure 5; and redraws the dataset and framework diagrams. It adds frame-count and attention plots, multiple diagnostic tables, and an expanded case gallery with masked imagery. Existing taxonomy and helpfulness displays are relocated or consolidated, alongside the conference-format layout change.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's evidence: Table 2 adds competing safety defenses and validates the framework beyond its original backbone, while Appendix E adds human verification of benchmark labels. Controlled analyses and disclosed reward weights strengthen interpretation and reproducibility, and the headline improvement arithmetic is corrected. Overstated cross-language conclusions and conflicting dataset-release statements remain weaknesses, but they do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation of the paper's central contributions.
